name: Agent-Based and Game Theory Models
title: Agent-Based and Game Theory Models
answer: Agent-based and game theory models in macroeconomic econometrics study economies as systems of interacting decision makers rather than as a single representative agent. Agent-based models specify households, firms, banks, and public authorities with heterogeneous rules, balance sheets, and expectations, then let macro outcomes such as growth, inflation, unemployment, and credit emerge from their interactions. Game theory models focus on strategic situations, including price setting, bargaining, auctions, policy games, and mechanism design, and ask what outcomes are stable when each party anticipates the others. In this field the two approaches often meet, because agent-based simulations need equilibrium concepts and game theory needs a realistic account of who the players are and how they learn. The scope therefore covers calibration, estimation, validation, and policy counterfactuals for questions that standard representative-agent models handle poorly, such as distributional effects, financial fragility, and coordination failures.

sections.body: Agent-based and game theory models in macroeconomic econometrics study economies as systems of interacting decision makers rather than as a single representative agent. Agent-based models specify households, firms, banks, and public authorities with heterogeneous rules, balance sheets, and expectations, then let macro outcomes such as growth, inflation, unemployment, and credit emerge from their interactions. Game theory models focus on strategic situations, including price setting, bargaining, auctions, policy games, and mechanism design, and ask what outcomes are stable when each party anticipates the others. In this field the two approaches often meet, because agent-based simulations need equilibrium concepts and game theory needs a realistic account of who the players are and how they learn. The scope therefore covers calibration, estimation, validation, and policy counterfactuals for questions that standard representative-agent models handle poorly, such as distributional effects, financial fragility, and coordination failures.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on ordinary scientific computing stacks, though large simulations benefit from clusters, cloud instances, and parallel processing. Agent-based platforms such as NetLogo, Mesa, Repast, and Agents.jl in Julia provide scheduling, spatial or network interaction, and logging, while Python, R, and MATLAB are common for custom code and analysis. Game theory work relies on optimization and equilibrium solvers, including linear programming, complementarity libraries, and tools such as Gambit for finite games. Data infrastructure matters as much as compute: national accounts, input-output tables, firm-level records, household surveys, and financial statements feed calibration and validation. Reproducibility usually depends on version control, container images, fixed random seeds, and documented parameter files.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a model design that states who the agents are, what they know, how they decide, and how they interact in markets or networks. Calibration and estimation then tie the model to data, often through method of simulated moments, indirect inference, Bayesian methods, or likelihood-free approaches such as approximate Bayesian computation. Game theory components are solved for equilibrium concepts such as Nash, subgame perfect, Bayesian Nash, or correlated equilibrium, with attention to multiple equilibria and equilibrium selection. Validation is a central step, using historical episodes, out-of-sample checks, micro-level patterns, sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo experiments to see whether the model reproduces facts it was not tuned to fit. Policy analysis then runs counterfactual scenarios, for example changes in taxes, interest rates, or macroprudential rules, and reports ranges rather than single point forecasts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area start with data provenance, because microdata, administrative records, and firm-level financial data carry licenses, confidentiality terms, and re-identification risks. Model provenance is equally important: code, parameter files, random seeds, and documentation should be versioned so that a result can be traced and reproduced. Risks include overfitting to a particular historical period, false precision from a single simulation run, hidden assumptions in agent rules, and policy conclusions that depend on an arbitrary equilibrium selection. Where models inform regulation or public policy, disclosure of limitations, sensitivity to assumptions, and independent review are common safeguards. The field also faces legal and ethical questions about automated decision rules, but those questions are handled through institutional review, data protection rules, and audit trails rather than through the models themselves.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward hybrid models that combine agent-based simulation with game theory, machine learning, and empirical macroeconometrics. Reinforcement learning agents, neural networks for expectations, and differentiable simulation are making it easier to estimate behavior from data rather than set it by hand. Faster hardware and GPU computing allow larger populations, richer networks, and many more scenario runs, which supports stress testing and digital twin style analysis. Central banks, finance ministries, and international organizations are likely to use these tools alongside DSGE and VAR models, not as a replacement. The open questions are validation, interpretability, and standardization, so that results can be compared across studies and used with appropriate caution.
